body:
Gujarat as a geological record

Gujarat contains rock formations and surface deposits belonging to widely separated geological intervals. Ancient crystalline rocks, marine sedimentary formations, volcanic basalt, younger petroleum-bearing sediments and recent alluvial deposits occur within the state.

Their different ages and origins explain many of Gujarat's distinctive landscapes and natural resources.

Ancient rocks of eastern and northeastern Gujarat

Parts of eastern and northeastern Gujarat contain ancient Precambrian crystalline and metamorphic formations associated with the geological development of Peninsular India.

Rocks related to the Aravalli and Delhi geological formations occur in northeastern Gujarat, including parts of the region adjoining Rajasthan. Granite, quartzite, schist and gneiss are examples of rocks found in these ancient geological regions.

Differences in rock resistance and prolonged erosion have contributed to the development of hills, ridges and valleys.

Jurassic marine fossils of Kachchh

During parts of the Mesozoic Era, marine waters occupied regions of the present Kachchh Basin. Sand, mud and other materials accumulated within these environments and subsequently formed sedimentary rocks.

Jurassic formations of Kachchh contain marine fossils such as ammonites, which were extinct marine molluscs with chambered shells.

Ammonite fossils are important because selected species can help identify the geological age of sedimentary layers. Their presence also demonstrates that areas now exposed on land were formerly marine environments.

Cretaceous dinosaur fossils at Raiyoli

Raiyoli, near Balasinor in Mahisagar district, is an important dinosaur fossil locality in Gujarat.

The area contains fossil evidence of dinosaurs, including eggs, eggshell fragments and skeletal remains. These fossils are associated with the Late Cretaceous geological history of western India.

The Lameta Formation, represented in parts of Gujarat and neighbouring regions, contains important Late Cretaceous dinosaur-bearing sedimentary deposits.

The fossils at Raiyoli demonstrate that the region supported terrestrial dinosaur populations before the end-Cretaceous mass extinction approximately 66 million years ago.

Kachchh's Jurassic ammonites primarily demonstrate ancient marine conditions. Raiyoli's Late Cretaceous dinosaur fossils demonstrate ancient terrestrial animal life and nesting activity.

Deccan Trap formations in Gujarat

Extensive Deccan Trap basalt occurs in parts of Saurashtra and southern Gujarat, including the Dang region. Related volcanic formations also occur elsewhere in the state.

Successive lava flows produced extensive basaltic rock formations around the end of the Cretaceous. Differential weathering and erosion of these flows contributed to the characteristic stepped appearance of several landscapes.

These rocks provide evidence of volcanic activity during the northward geological movement of the Indian landmass.

Younger sedimentary formations and petroleum

The Cambay Basin, also called the Khambhat Basin, is an important petroleum-bearing sedimentary basin of western India.

Its geological development involved the formation of a rift basin, where subsidence created space for sediments to accumulate. Younger sedimentary formations developed above the Deccan volcanic rocks.

Burial and transformation of organic matter in suitable sedimentary environments contributed to petroleum and natural gas formation. These resources accumulated within favourable subsurface rock formations.

Gujarat also contains lignite deposits associated with younger sedimentary formations. Lignite is a relatively low-rank coal and must be distinguished from the major older Gondwana coal deposits of eastern and central India.

Recent alluvium and coastal deposits

Gujarat's extensive mainland plains contain younger sediments deposited by rivers. The Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada and Tapi river systems have contributed to the development of alluvial landscapes.

The Rann of Kachchh and other coastal lowlands contain comparatively young sediments shaped by river deposition, marine processes, tidal activity and changes in relative land and sea levels.

These environments illustrate how geological processes continue to modify Gujarat's surface even though some of its underlying rocks are extremely ancient.

Gujarat's geological history in chronological order

Prelims focus

  • Precambrian: ancient crystalline and metamorphic rocks of eastern and northeastern Gujarat.
  • Jurassic: important marine ammonite-bearing formations of Kachchh.
  • Late Cretaceous: dinosaur fossils at Raiyoli near Balasinor.
  • End-Cretaceous transition: extensive Deccan Trap basalt in parts of Saurashtra and southern Gujarat.
  • Cenozoic sedimentary formations: petroleum-bearing Cambay Basin and younger lignite deposits.
  • Recent geological intervals: river alluvium, tidal flats and coastal deposits.

Trap: A fossil-bearing sedimentary formation and a basaltic lava flow represent different geological processes, even when their ages are relatively close.

[References: Geological Survey of India, Gujarat Briefing Book, Introduction and regional geological framework; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Navnirman Special Issue, 1985, Geomorphology and geological formations, hosted by the Government of Gujarat; Directorate General of Hydrocarbons, National Data Repository, Cambay Basin, Age of the Basin and Sediment Thickness; Desai and Patel, Upper Callovian-Middle Oxfordian Belemnite Assemblage from Jara Dome, Western Kachchh, Journal of the Geological Society of India, 2009, pp. 343–356; Gujarat Tourism, Kutch Desert Sanctuary and Balasinor Dinosaur Museum; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 7, p. 80. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
